Yes — this is possible. The key term is “multi-seat X” or “multiseat”.

You can set up one PC for two users with separate keyboards, mice, and monitors, running independent sessions at the same time. Common approaches are:

- Multiple X servers
- Xephyr on top of Xorg

Which works best depends on your hardware, Xorg version, and distribution. You may also need to configure the display manager and audio separately.

Search for Ubuntu/Debian/Gentoo/Arch “multiseat” guides, and check the Xorg multiseat documentation.

`last` is showing a time change, not a real TTY name.

The `|` and `{` entries in the TTY field mean the system clock was adjusted automatically:
- `|` = time before the change
- `{` = time after the change

This comes from `utmp`/`wtmp` records and usually indicates NTP or another time sync corrected the system time.

Yes—use separate X servers/sessions and run GNOME per display. For example, start one X session on `:0` for the local seat and another on `:1` for the second seat, then launch GNOME against each display:

```sh
DISPLAY=:0 gnome-session
DISPLAY=:1 gnome-session
```

Or configure a display manager like GDM for multi-seat. In practice, for GNOME 3 the recommended way is to let `gdm`/systemd-logind handle seats, and assign each seat to its own GPU/input devices. If you’re using Xming, set it to “single window” mode only if you want everything inside one window; otherwise use full-screen/windowed separate X displays.

`last` doesn’t use the same “TTY” meaning as `ps`. In `last`, the TTY field is taken from the login session record, and if no real terminal was attached or the record is malformed/placeholder, you can see symbols like `{` or `|`.

Those characters are not actual terminal names; they usually indicate an unknown, synthetic, or non-terminal session source in the wtmp/utmp database.

So:
- `ps` `TIME` = CPU time used
- `last` `TTY` = recorded terminal for the login session, which can be a placeholder like `{` or `|` if no real TTY was stored.

Yes — in Synergy you can bind a hotkey to switch focus to a specific screen.

Add a `section: options` entry like this:

```ini
section: options
    keystroke(alt+right) = switchToScreen(hp7)
    keystroke(alt+down)  = switchToScreen(optiplex-380)
    keystroke(alt+left)  = switchToScreen(laptop)
end
```

Then use `switchToScreen(<screen-name>)` for each machine. This lets you jump between computers without moving the mouse.

If you want a true “cycle through all windows/apps everywhere” behavior, Synergy itself doesn’t manage windows across machines that way; it only switches keyboard/mouse focus between screens.

GNOME 3 does not normally manage multiple independent X screens well. GNOME Shell is designed for one X screen/compositor session, not true multiseat-style separate shells per X screen.

What to do instead:
- **Best option:** use **separate X servers** (one per seat/display), not multiple X screens in one X server.
- If you must use multiple X screens, you can start a shell per screen manually, e.g.:
  `DISPLAY=:0.1 gnome-shell --replace`
  but this is fragile and not a supported setup.
- For multiseat, use **systemd-logind / GDM multiseat** so each seat gets its own Xorg + GNOME session.

Also, disable **Xinerama** only if you’re using separate X screens; GNOME may still only fully support the primary screen.

GNOME 3 doesn’t have a simple built-in “multiseat setup” wizard. The usual approach is to configure multiseat at the system level, then start separate X sessions for each seat.

Typical options:
- Use systemd/logind multiseat support
- Create udev rules to assign each keyboard/mouse/GPU to a seat
- Run one X server per seat, then launch a GNOME session on each display

If you want the easiest path, a distro with good hardware support and up-to-date X/DRI stack helps. In the referenced thread, Sabayon or Gentoo were suggested because they’re more likely to have the needed GPU and Xorg support.

For GNOME 3 specifically, multiseat is usually done by combining:
- separate seats
- separate Xorg configs or auto-detection
- separate login sessions per seat

If the process is still running, you can inspect it with:

ps axho etime,cmd

But for processes that already exited, there’s no reliable built-in “last 10 seconds” command-history view unless you had auditing enabled beforehand.

What you can sometimes infer is recent file access from executed binaries, e.g.:

find ${PATH//:/ } -type f -amin -1

This only works if the executable was actually read from disk and not served from cache, and it won’t always tell you the exact command line.

For exact hindsight command execution, use a logger/auditing tool in advance, such as auditd, process accounting, or shell history logging.

Yes — use the shell builtin `time` before the command:

```sh
time make
```

It will print how long the command took after it finishes.

If you want a more detailed breakdown, some shells support `\time` or `/usr/bin/time -v`:

```sh
/usr/bin/time -v make
```

For “in hindsight” on a command you already ran, you generally need shell history with timestamps enabled beforehand; otherwise the exact duration isn’t recoverable.

On OpenSUSE 12.1, `inittab` is not the right startup mechanism because the system uses `systemd`, not classic SysV init.

So your `respawn` line in `inittab` will be ignored or won’t behave as expected. Create a systemd service instead, for example:

`/etc/systemd/system/myprogname.service`
```ini
[Unit]
Description=My progname service

[Service]
ExecStart=/home/bits/MyProgram/start.myprogram
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Then run:
```sh
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable myprogname.service
systemctl start myprogname.service
```

Also note: `Restart=restart-always` should be `Restart=always`.

If a background job is trying to read from stdin, the shell suspends it with `SIGTTIN`. That’s why it “stops” until you bring it to the foreground.

To control jobs in a shell:

- Suspend foreground job: `Ctrl+Z`
- List jobs: `jobs`
- Bring job to foreground: `fg %1`
- Resume in background: `bg %1`

For your Ant case, the usual fix is to prevent it from reading stdin when run in the background, e.g. run it with stdin redirected:

```sh
ant -f myfile.xml </dev/null &> foo.out &
```

Ant is known to try to read stdin immediately in some cases.

To suspend a foreground job, press:

- `Ctrl+Z` → stops the process and returns you to the shell

To bring it back:

- `fg` → resumes it in the foreground
- `bg` → resumes it in the background

If you want to see jobs:

- `jobs`

Example:

```sh
sleep 100
# press Ctrl+Z
bg
fg
```

If your goal is to keep running a command repeatedly in the background, `watch` is usually not the right tool. Use a loop instead:

```sh
while true; do
  cmd >> output.txt
  sleep 2
done
```

To suspend a foreground process, press Ctrl+Z. That sends it a stop signal, and you can then resume it in the background with:

bg

To bring a background job back to the foreground, use:

fg

If you have multiple jobs, list them with:

jobs

Then bring a specific one back with:

fg %1

or resume one in the background with:

bg %1

You generally can’t send a running foreground app to the background instantly without a brief stop; the shell/terminal job-control model requires a suspend/resume step.

Fedora is the upstream, community-driven project where new features are introduced and tested quickly. Red Hat’s server-focused, long-term supported product is RHEL, which is the “server edition” in that ecosystem.

So the short answer is: Fedora doesn’t have a separate server edition because Fedora itself isn’t positioned as a stable, long-life server product. It’s meant to feed into RHEL. If you want a Fedora-based server OS, Fedora Server exists today as a Fedora spin, but for traditional enterprise server use, RHEL or a compatible rebuild like CentOS Stream/AlmaLinux/Rocky is usually the closer fit.

In BusyBox `inittab`, the leading `-` before `/bin/ash` means start the shell as a **login shell**.

So:

`console::askfirst:-/bin/ash`

tells BusyBox `init` to run `/bin/ash` with `argv[0]` starting with `-`, which many shells interpret as “login shell.” That usually changes which startup files are read, such as `~/.profile`.

This `-` is a BusyBox-specific convention and is different from the `+` accounting flag mentioned in some man pages.

For a Linux-compatible external drive, use a Linux filesystem like ext4 (best for Linux-only use) or FAT32/exFAT if you need cross-platform compatibility.

Typical steps:

1. Find the device name:
`lsblk`

2. Unmount any mounted partitions:
`sudo umount /dev/sdX1`

3. Create a partition if needed:
`sudo fdisk /dev/sdX`

4. Format it:
`sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdX1`

If you want broader compatibility with Windows/macOS too, use FAT32:
`sudo mkfs.vfat /dev/sdX1`

Be very careful to use the correct disk (`/dev/sdX`), or you can erase the wrong drive.

Fedora does have a Server edition, but it’s not always shown as a separate “big” download like Ubuntu Server.

What Fedora typically provides is:
- a Netinstall image, or
- a standard installer image

During installation, you can choose the Server role/package set. That’s why it may seem like there isn’t a separate server ISO.

So the difference is mostly packaging and presentation:
- Ubuntu: separate Desktop/Server images
- Fedora: one installer, with Server as an install choice

If you want a server-style Fedora install, use the netinstall or standard installer and select the Server option during setup.

To format an external drive for Linux, use a Linux filesystem like ext4.

Be careful: this erases all data on the drive.

Example commands:

```bash
lsblk
sudo umount /dev/sdX1
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdX1
```

Replace `/dev/sdX1` with your actual partition.

If you want a script that finds media-mounted drives and formats them, the resolved thread used:

```bash
while read -r line; do
  mkfs.ext4 "$line"
done < <(df -k | grep 'media' | cut -d ' ' -f 1)
```

This is useful on systems where external drives mount under `/media`.

If the drive will be used only on Linux, format it with a Linux-native filesystem. For best general use, btrfs is a good choice, especially if you want data integrity features and flexibility. ext4 is also a very solid, simple option if you want maximum compatibility and low maintenance.

If you need Windows access too, consider NTFS or exFAT instead, since Linux filesystems like ext4/btrfs are not natively readable by Windows without extra software.

So:
- Linux only: btrfs or ext4
- Linux + Windows: NTFS or exFAT

For an external hard drive, ext4 is often the safest default unless you specifically want btrfs features.

For a Linux-only external drive, ext4 is usually the best choice: it’s stable, fast, and well-supported.

Permission issues only happen if the same usernames/groups don’t map to the same UID/GID numbers across machines. ext4 stores numeric ownership, so “alice” on one system may not be the same UID on another.

Ways to avoid trouble:
- Keep the same user/UID across your Linux machines.
- Or mount the drive with a consistent ownership via `/etc/fstab` using `uid=` and `gid=` options for filesystems that support them.
- If you want more cross-system flexibility, UDF is an option, but it’s less common and somewhat experimental compared to ext4.

For most Linux users: ext4 is the right answer.

Yes. The drive itself doesn’t need to be “Windows” or “Linux” specific.

What matters is the filesystem on the drive. Linux can usually read/write NTFS, FAT32, exFAT, and native Linux filesystems like ext4. For best Linux use, ext4 is a good choice if you’ll mainly use it on Linux. If you also need Windows access, exFAT is often the easiest shared option.

Notes:
- NFS is a network filesystem, not a disk format.
- FAT32 has a 4 GB file size limit, so avoid it for large simulation data.
- For 1 TB, USB3 or direct SATA will be much faster than USB2.

If you have the patch ID/commit, the easiest way is to look at the commit in the kernel git web interface:

1. Open the commit/patch page.
2. Click commitdiff.
3. Click raw.
4. Check the `X-Git-Tag` header.

That header tells you which tagged kernel release contains the fix. If it’s not in a release tag yet, it hasn’t been included in an official kernel release.

If you need an external drive that works reasonably well across Linux, macOS, and Windows without extra drivers, UDF is a good choice.

Why UDF:
- Supported out of the box on Linux (2.6.31+)
- Supported on Windows Vista and newer
- Supported on macOS
- Better fit than FAT for modern large drives

On Linux, you can create it with:
- `mkudffs` from the `udftools` package

One caveat: UDF support varies by version across platforms, so pick a broadly compatible version if you need maximum interoperability.

To list Windows/Samba shares on the local network from a Linux terminal, you can use:

```bash
smbclient -L //WINDOWS_PC_IP -U username
```

If you want to browse by hostname or find hosts first:

```bash
nmblookup -A IP_ADDRESS
```

To access a share, mount it to a local directory:

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/smbshare
sudo mount -t cifs //WINDOWS_PC_IP/ShareName /mnt/smbshare -o username=name,password=password
```

Then use `cd`, `ls`, etc. on `/mnt/smbshare`.

If you want, I can also show how to discover all SMB hosts automatically on a subnet.

To list Windows shared folders (Samba) on your local network, first find the active hosts, then query SMB shares.

Common ways:

- `nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24` to discover hosts
- `nmap --script smb-enum-shares -p 445 192.168.1.0/24` to enumerate shares
- `smbclient -L //<host> -U <user>` to list shares on a specific machine
- `smbtree` to browse SMB workgroup/domain shares

If you’re not sure of the subnet, check DHCP for your IP, gateway, and netmask first. Then scan only networks you’re authorized to test.

To list Windows/Samba shared folders available on the local network, use one of these:

- On Windows: open File Explorer and type  
  `\\servername` or `\\IP-address`  
  This shows available shares on that host.

- From Linux/macOS terminal:
  `smbclient -L //server -U username`
  or for guest access:
  `smbclient -L //server -N`

- To browse the whole local network, use a network browser tool (Windows Network, `nmap`, or Samba discovery), but note browsing depends on network discovery being enabled.

If you can see the share but not its contents, the Samba user/guest account likely lacks Unix filesystem permissions, or SELinux is blocking access.

In `top`, press `e` to cycle the memory units shown in the summary and fields. It will switch to human-friendly units like K, M, G, etc., so `RES` can appear in megabytes.

If you want to keep it that way, press `W` to save the settings to your `~/.toprc`.

You can also press `?` in `top` for more options.

In top, memory values are shown in KiB by default, not MB.

You can switch the display unit interactively:
- Press `E` to cycle summary memory units
- Press `e` to cycle task memory units

On many versions of `top`, `E` changes the header/meminfo display scale to KiB/MB/GB depending on your version, and `e` affects per-process memory fields.

If you want MB consistently, you can also start top with a different unit setting if supported by your version (some versions have `-E` options), but the exact flags vary by implementation. Check `man top` for your system.

In `top`, memory is usually shown in kilobytes by default. To make it easier to read in megabytes:

1. Start `top`
2. Press `E` (uppercase) to cycle the memory summary/unit display
3. Keep pressing until it shows `MiB` or `MB` depending on your version

If you mean the process list sorting by memory usage, press:

- `Shift + M` to sort by `%MEM`

If your `top` doesn’t support unit toggling, you may need to use another tool like `htop` for more flexible display.

This is usually a permissions/ID-mapping issue on the NFS mount, not NIS itself.

Check these on both server and client:

1. NFS export permissions
- Ensure `/home/guest/nis1` is exported with the right options.
- Verify client is allowed in `/etc/exports`.

2. Directory ownership and mode
- On the NFS server:
  - `ls -ld /home/guest/nis1`
- The NIS user must have matching UID/GID on server and client.
- If the directory or `.bash_profile` is not readable/executable by that UID, you’ll get “Permission denied”.

3. Autofs mount options
- Check `/etc/auto.*` and make sure the mount is actually happening.
- Test with `mount` and `showmount -e server`.

4. SELinux / firewall
- Temporarily test with SELinux disabled or set permissive.

5. Verify user identity
- `id nis1`
- Confirm the home directory in NIS matches the NFS path.

Yes — use a relative rpath with `$ORIGIN`.

If you link the executable with something like:

`-Wl,-rpath,'$ORIGIN/../lib'`

then the loader will look for shared libraries relative to the executable’s location, for example:

- executables in `<base>/bin/`
- libraries in `<base>/lib/`

This gives you a private library path for just that executable, without needing `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` or system-wide `ld.so.conf.d` changes.

`-L` and `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` serve different stages:

- `-L...` is for the linker at compile/link time, so `gcc -lrtadb -L/path/to/lib`
- `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` is for the runtime loader, so the app can find the shared library when you run it

If you want system-wide use without setting `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, adding the directory to `/etc/ld.so.conf.d/*.conf` and running `ldconfig` is the right approach.

For your compile command, you still need `-L` if the library isn’t in a default link path:

`gcc myapp.c -lrtadb -L/usr/local/lib/rta-0.8.1/src`

Also make sure the library file is actually named like `librtadb.so` and that the path you added is the directory containing it.

Mono is trying to load libX11.so.6 from the wrong place, so it’s likely a broken/misconfigured Mono install or a missing X11 runtime package.

Try this:

1. Install the X11 libraries:
   apt-get install libx11-6

2. Reinstall Mono packages:
   apt-get install --reinstall mono-complete

3. Check whether the file exists:
   ls -l /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libX11.so.6

If the app still fails, it may be a Wine/.NET app that shouldn’t be run with mono directly. In that case run it under Wine instead of `mono app.exe`.

Yes, they can usually be synchronized, assuming they’re using the same directory service software/protocol and compatible replication settings. In a mixed RHEL 6 / CentOS 5 environment, replication is often possible because the underlying DS is effectively the same product family.

A few cautions:
- Verify the exact DS version/replication topology; cross-version replication may have limitations.
- Add the Samba schema to both servers if you want the replicated environment to remain consistent. If one server lacks the schema, entries using that schema may not replicate cleanly or may be ignored/produce errors.
- Test in a staging setup first.

A good choice is Capistrano.

It’s a Ruby-based utility/framework for running commands on multiple remote Linux machines over SSH, and it already handles much of the connection, execution, and parallelization work for you.

If you want something simpler or more shell-based, you could also use:
- ssh + a loop in a shell script
- Ansible for larger-scale automation
- pdsh for parallel command execution

But for the exact need of “run a local script that connects to various servers and runs commands,” Capistrano is a solid fit.

Yes—if by “synchronised” you mean keeping servers on the same configuration, that’s commonly done with configuration management tools like Ansible, Puppet, Chef, or Salt. They can push the same settings to multiple servers over SSH and help keep them consistent.

From the thread context: if you’re changing network settings remotely, use a script that applies the change, then verifies connectivity (for example, ping the management server). If verification fails, roll back to the previous config. That reduces the risk of locking yourself out.

So: yes, servers can be kept in sync, but do it with automation and a rollback/check step for risky changes.

If the machines don’t have build tools, don’t compile on them. Build once on a compatible system and deploy the resulting binary packages.

Best approach:
1. Create proper Debian binary packages from the ALSA source.
2. Put those packages in an APT repository.
3. Install/update them on the client machines with `apt`.

In other words, backport the package for Debian 6 (“squeeze”) and distribute it as a repo, rather than using `checkinstall` or copying files manually. `checkinstall` is often unreliable for this.

If some machines lose soundcard detection, that’s likely a separate driver/configuration issue, not just packaging.

Use SSH restrictions rather than trying to “hide” the whole system with a normal shell.

Best options:
- In `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, use `command="..."` to force a single allowed command or wrapper script.
- Set the user’s shell to a restricted shell, e.g. `rbash`, or use a custom restricted shell.
- Put the user in a chroot jail or container if you need filesystem isolation from other directories.
- For CPU/memory limits, use `ulimit`, PAM limits, or cgroups/CGroups.

If the goal is “SSH in, but only run screen/irssi and only see home,” combine:
1. forced command or wrapper,
2. chroot jail,
3. resource limits.

For deploying to multiple machines, consider using a deployment tool rather than custom SSH/rsync scripts.

Good options:
- Fabric (Python-based): automate SSH commands, file transfers, and orchestration.
- Capistrano (Ruby-based): common for multi-server deployments and release management.

If your current approach is a push model, that’s fine for many setups. A pull model can help when machines should fetch updates themselves, but it depends on your environment and operational needs.

If you want, I can also suggest tools based on your stack (Python, Linux, containers, etc.).

For multiple CentOS 6.5 machines, the most maintainable options are:

1. Package it as an RPM
- Best for repeatable installs, upgrades, and rollback.
- Create your own RPM from the upstream spec, bump the version, and host it in a small internal repo.
- Deploy with yum on each workstation.

2. If you want a shared installation
- Install under a versioned path like /usr/local/companyname/.
- For libraries, you can centralize them on NFS, but this can be fragile if networking changes or if clients need different versions.

Best practice: build an RPM and distribute it through an internal yum repository. That scales much better than copying files manually.

Yes. To replicate basic config tasks, keep your current `.config` and reuse it on the newer kernel source tree:

- Copy `.config` into the new kernel build directory
- Run `make oldconfig` to update it for new options
- Or run `make menuconfig` and just save/exit without changing anything

`make oldconfig` is the usual unattended way, since it prompts only for new settings.  
`make menuconfig` also updates the config even if you don’t edit anything.  

This preserves your existing choices while adapting to new kernel versions.

Yes—use Kickstart, not just for installation but also for post-install setup.

Create:
- a Kickstart file for partitioning, package selection, and base install
- a `%post` section to run scripts after install
- scripts on a Kickstart server to handle basic configuration, software setup, and customization

This lets you install and configure all 15 machines consistently and much faster than doing them one by one. The initial setup effort pays off quickly. Red Hat’s Kickstart documentation is a good reference.

Ubuntu does not use space on an unmounted hard disk.

To see what disks are in the system, use:

- `lsblk` — lists disks and partitions
- `sudo fdisk -l` — shows all detected drives and partition tables
- `blkid` — shows labels and UUIDs for partitions
- `dmesg | grep -i sd` — shows disk detection messages

Example:

```bash
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MOUNTPOINT,MODEL
```

If a disk seems “missing” under `/dev/sdX`, it may still be mounted by label or UUID, so `blkid` is useful to match names to devices.

A simple way is to use a boot-time startup script launched after networking/services are up, then trigger your configuration tool from it.

In the resolved example, the suggested approach was UbuntuPostInstall, which supports:
- running non-interactively at startup
- pre/post actions for custom scripts
- console output/logging
- reading a local config file or downloading one from the network

You could also:
1. Create a system init/service job to run your script on first boot
2. Make the script idempotent so it can safely rerun
3. Log output with `tee` so it appears on console and in a file
4. Prompt only on errors if needed

On Linux, the simplest ways are:

- `lsscsi -g` — shows SCSI devices and often the disk model
- `cat /proc/scsi/scsi` — lists attached SCSI devices
- `udevadm info --query=all --name=/dev/sdX | grep -E 'ID_MODEL|ID_VENDOR'`
- `smartctl -i /dev/sdX` — usually shows make/model if the controller exposes the disks

If you’re behind a RAID controller, you may only see the RAID volume (like the 3ware controller), not the individual physical disks. In that case, use the RAID management tool for your controller (for 3ware, `tw_cli` or `3dm2`) to list the physical drives and their make/model.

To see what hard disks are in the system:

Linux:
- `lsblk` — lists disks and partitions
- `sudo fdisk -l` — shows all detected disks, sizes, and sector counts
- `sudo lshw -class disk` — detailed hardware info

Example:
- `sudo fdisk -l /dev/sda`
  - shows the disk size and total number of sectors

Windows:
- Open Disk Management: `diskmgmt.msc`
- Or use Command Prompt:
  - `wmic diskdrive get model,size`
- Or PowerShell:
  - `Get-Disk`

If you specifically want sector info, `fdisk -l` on Linux is the usual way to get the total sectors.

Yes. You can identify the installed HDD/SSD from the command line.

Try:

```bash
mount
```

This shows mounted filesystems. The root filesystem line tells you the main drive, e.g. `/dev/sda1 on /`.

Then map that device to the actual disk with:

```bash
sudo lshw -class disk
```

or:

```bash
sudo fdisk -l
```

Example: if `mount` shows `/dev/sda1`, then `lshw` or `fdisk` will tell you whether `/dev/sda` is a Toshiba, Seagate, etc., and its size/serial.

Yes. On Debian/Linux you can check installed HDDs with:


In practice, Debian/apt and Arch/pacman solve the same basic problem, but with different priorities.

`>` redirects output to a file, overwriting/truncating that file if it already exists.

`>>` redirects output to a file by appending to the end of it.

With `cat`:
- `cat file1 > file2` = copy contents of `file1` into `file2`, replacing whatever was there
- `cat file1 >> file2` = add `file1`’s contents to the end of `file2`

`>\>` is not a special append operator. The backslash escapes the second `>`, so the shell treats it like a literal character/name, which is why it can behave like a file named `>`.

So yes: for appending, use `>>`.

`>` redirects stdout to a file, creating/truncating it. `>>` appends stdout to the end of a file, creating it if it doesn’t exist.

With `cat`:

- `cat a > b` means “read `a` and write it to `b`, replacing `b`”
- `cat a >> b` means “read `a` and append it to the end of `b`”

So `>` is like overwrite, `>>` is like add-on.

Related to `cat`, `cat a > b` is often used to copy a file, but `cp a b` is the proper tool and is usually faster and safer.

- `>>` redirects output to a file, appending to it if it exists.
  - Example: `echo hello >> out.txt`

- `cat file1 >> all.txt` → append `file1` to the end of `all.txt`

In bash, redirection changes a command’s file descriptors.

- `< file` sends a file to the command’s standard input.
- `> file` sends the command’s standard output to a file.
- `2>` redirects standard error.
- `>> file` appends output to a file.
- `|` connects the standard output of one command to the standard input of another using a pipe.

So the key difference is:
- `<` connects a file to stdin
- `|` connects one program’s output to another program’s input

Also, `|` typically runs commands in a pipeline/subshell, while simple redirection does not.

In bash, use a pipeline or process substitution depending on what you want.

If you want the output of multiple commands to become input to another command:

(command1; command2 | grep pattern) | command3

Or with a group:

{ command1; command2 | grep pattern; } | command3

If the receiving command expects a file argument, use process substitution:

command3 < <(command1; command2 | grep pattern)

If you’re just passing text as stdin, a pipeline is usually the right tool.  
If you’re putting command output into arguments, use command substitution: `echo "$(date)"`.

From `man cut`:
- “Selected input is written in the same order that it is read.”

If you need reordering, `cut` isn’t the right tool. Use something like `awk`, `sed`, or a small script to rearrange characters.

```bash

command |

  awk '{print $3}' |
```

So: one branch is easy; combining both with `paste` requires a FIFO.

Linux kernel headers are the C header files that define the kernel’s interface and internal data structures. They include things like system call numbers, kernel APIs, constants, structs, and architecture-specific definitions.

In the source tree, the split usually means:

- `include/linux/`: generic kernel headers used across architectures

```bash
  else
    a[$1] = second $2 ";" third $3
}
END { for (i in a) print i ";" a[i] }' is2.txt
```

The main `/etc/passwd` is the system user database.

`passwd-` is usually just a backup copy of `/etc/passwd` created by tools like `vipw` or package scripts, for example:

- `/etc/passwd` = active file
- `/etc/passwd-` = backup/previous version

In your case, the issue is likely that `/etc/passwd` was edited with Windows line endings (`CRLF`), so root’s shell became `/bin/bash\r` instead of `/bin/bash`.

`/etc/passwd` is the standard user account database file. It’s usually world-readable and contains account info in colon-separated fields.

`/etc/passwd-` is typically just a backup copy of `/etc/passwd` created by tools like `vipw` or `pwconv` before editing/converting. The trailing `-` is not part of a Unix standard; it’s a convention used by some systems.

So:

- `/etc/passwd` = active file
- `/etc/passwd-` = backup/previous version

It may not exist on all systems, and its meaning can vary by distro/tool.

`/etc/shadow` is the active password hash file.  
`/etc/shadow-` is a backup copy of the previous version, created by the shadow-utils tools when the file is edited or updated.

Same pattern exists for:
- `/etc/passwd-`
- `/etc/group-`
- `/etc/gshadow-`

These backups help recover from a bad edit or failed update. If your system created them, that usually indicates normal user/account management activity, not malware.

`/etc/shadow` does not store the password itself; it stores a hash of the password for each account.

Even if two users have the same plaintext password, their hashes can still be different because the hash process usually includes a per-user random salt. That salt makes the result unique and prevents attackers from spotting matching passwords easily.

So:

- root and your user are different accounts
- each account has its own shadow entry
- same password ≠ same hash
- it’s usually the same algorithm, but with different salts

There isn’t a built-in “move file and automatically retarget all symlinks” command.

If you want to keep the same symlink names, you can update them in place with:

```sh
mv oldfile newdir/newfile
ln -sf newdir/newfile existinglink
```

`ln -sf` forces the symlink to point to the new target.

1. move the file
2. create a new symlink to the new location
3. leave the old symlink until you’re ready to remove it

If you just want to move a file and leave a symlink behind, the fish function from the resolved thread does that:

```fish
function lnmv
    set dest_dir $argv[1]
    set files $argv[2..-1]

    for f in $files
        set dest $dest_dir/$f
        mv -- $f $dest
        and ln -s -- $dest $f
    end
end
```

Usage:

```fish
lnmv /new/location file1 file2
```

This moves each file into `/new/location/` and creates a symlink at the original path.

So if you move `/old/path/file` to `/new/path/file`, symlinks still point to `/old/path/file` and become broken unless their text is updated.

To update all symlinks, you must find links whose target matches the old path and rewrite them to the new path. There is no universal automatic retargeting by `mv`.

Zombie processes have little to no practical impact. They’ve already exited, so they do not use RAM or CPU and have deallocated their memory. They do still occupy a process table entry until their parent reaps them, but that’s usually the only resource involved and it’s minimal.

So, reaping zombies is mostly about cleaning up the process table and keeping the system tidy. If you have lots of zombies, it can indicate a bug in the parent process, but the zombies themselves aren’t consuming significant resources.

Use `--` to stop the command from treating `-` as an option.

For a directory named `-`:

If that doesn’t work in your shell, you can also use a relative path:

The `--` form is the safest and most general.

Reaping a zombie has little direct impact on system resources, because a zombie is already dead and uses no CPU, memory, or open files.

The main impact is reclaiming the process table entry. If zombies are left unreaped, they can accumulate and eventually consume PID/process-table slots, which can prevent new processes from being created.

So:
- No meaningful runtime cost from the zombie itself
- Yes, you should reap them to avoid exhausting process table/PID resources

In short: zombies are harmless individually, but lots of unreaped zombies can become a problem.

A `kill -9` can’t kill a process that’s stuck in uninterruptible sleep (`D` state), usually waiting on I/O, NFS, a hung device, or a kernel lock. That’s why it can look “murder proof.”

What to do:
- Try `kill -TERM <pid>` first, then `kill -INT`.
- Check the process state: `ps -o pid,stat,wchan,cmd -p <pid>`
- Investigate the wait: `strace -p <pid>` (or `truss`, `ltrace`, `gdb`, `pstack`)
- Look for stalled storage/network mounts, device errors, or kernel logs (`dmesg`).

If it’s in `D` state, restarting the underlying I/O subsystem or fixing the kernel wait is usually the real solution.

- You’re trying to kill PID 1, which even root can’t SIGKILL

If it’s in `D` state, `kill -9` is queued but won’t take effect until the kernel call returns. Check with:

`ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p <pid>`

- `df`/used space shows filesystem metadata, not just your files
- ext4 always consumes some space
- `lazy_itable_init=1` speeds formatting, but doesn’t reduce final metadata usage

- **Reserved blocks**: Unix filesystems often reserve space for root/system use, so `used + avail` may not equal `total`.
- **Rounding**: `df -h` uses human-readable units, so values are rounded and may not add up precisely.
- **Metadata / overhead**: Journals, inode tables, superblocks, etc. consume space but aren’t always obvious in “used” figures.
- **Different definitions**: `used` may include space not visible to normal users, while `avail` excludes reserved space.

So a mismatch is usually normal. If you want exact block counts, use `df -B1` or `df -B512`.

- Reserved blocks: ext4 keeps some blocks reserved for root/system use.
- Rounding: values are often shown in human units, so displayed numbers may not add up exactly.
- Delayed allocation / filesystem behavior: what’s “used” can include space not directly tied to files.

For ext4, `df` gets these numbers from the filesystem superblock/block counters, so it’s fast and approximate at the display level, not a literal file-by-file total.

Some space can be “used” even when a filesystem looks empty because filesystems reserve space for metadata and internal structures.

Common reasons:
- Superblock, inode tables, journal, and allocation bitmaps
- Reserved blocks for root/admin use
- Block size/alignment overhead, so small files still consume at least one block
- Extra features on newer filesystems, like journaling and extents
- Hidden or special files, snapshots, or lost+found
- Sparse files: after restore, they may become fully allocated and use much more real disk space

So `df` reports space consumed by both file contents and filesystem overhead, not just visible files.

```sh
sed -E ':a; s/"([^"]*);([^"]*)"/"\1,\2"/g; ta' file
```

- Serialize with `flock`

Some space is intentionally reserved by the filesystem, even when it looks empty.

On ext filesystems, a default percentage is set aside mainly for:
- root/admin processes, so the system can still log in, repair, or recover when the disk is nearly full
- performance, because fragmentation gets much worse when the filesystem is above about 95% full

So `df` shows less usable space than the raw capacity. This is normal, and you can change the reserved percentage with `tune2fs -m`. For archive-like storage, the reserved space may matter less.

On Linux, “executable” is not about the file being a special kind of file by name; it’s mostly about the executable permission bit.

There are two common executable types:

- Binaries: compiled into a format like ELF. The kernel loads and runs them directly.
- Scripts: plain text files with a shebang like #!/bin/bash. The kernel starts the interpreter, which reads the script.

Compilation and linking still matter because they turn source code into machine code, resolve symbols, and package everything into a form the CPU can run efficiently. The final binary depends on libraries and system ABI, so portability is limited by those dependencies. Source code is portable in principle, but the compiled executable usually is not.

```sh

while IFS= read -r f; do
  d=${f%/*}
  base=${f##*/}
  name=${base%.*}
  ext=${base##*.}
  ext=$(printf '%s' "$ext" | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z')

done
```

`command` and `$(command)` are not the same thing.

```sh
echo ls
# prints: ls

# prints the files listed by ls
```

- use `$(command)` when you want its output as text in another command

POSIX does not define “long options” like `--help`.

POSIX option syntax is basically:
- one dash `-`
- followed by a single alphanumeric option character

So `-a`, `-l`, `-f` are POSIX-style options. POSIX also reserves `-W` for vendor use, but it still doesn’t standardize long options.

`--` is not a POSIX long-option marker; it’s mostly a GNU convention. In many commands, a bare `--` means “end of options” so later arguments are treated as operands, not options.

When you type a command in the shell, the shell:

1. reads the line you entered,
2. splits it into words/arguments,
3. looks for the command (built-in, function, or executable in $PATH),
4. runs it, usually as a new process,
5. waits for it to finish and then shows the next prompt.

In an interactive terminal, your shell is just doing this live. A script does the same thing, but from a file, and it runs in a new shell process, so changes like variable assignments usually do not affect your current shell.

When you type a command in a shell, the shell usually:

1. reads and parses the command
2. checks whether it’s a built-in
3. if it’s external, creates a child process with fork/clone
4. in the child, replaces the program image with execve
5. the parent waits for the child to finish

So for a simple external command like `ls`, you typically see fork/clone + execve.

To trace this, use:

`strace -f -e trace=process bash -c 'ls; :'`

`-f` follows child processes, and `trace=process` shows process-creation calls. The `:` is important because with only one command, bash may optimize by doing a direct execve instead of forking.

When you type a command on the shell, the shell:

1. Parses the line into words.
2. Expands variables, globs, etc.
3. Looks up the command name in PATH if needed.
4. Starts a new process to run it, passing arguments to that process.

You can do this with a shell script that groups files by the “base” part before the trailing number, then renames each group in numeric order.

Example approach:

```sh
current=
numbers=
i=0

for x in *.txt ''; do
  stem=${x%.*}
  n=${stem##*[!0-9]}
  stem=${stem%$n}

    for k in $(printf '%s\n' $numbers | sort -n); do
      y=${i}_${k}.txt
      mv "$current$k.txt" "$y"
    done
    current=$stem
    numbers=$n
    i=$((i+1))
  else
    numbers="$numbers $n"
  fi
done
```

What’s happening is that `*(pattern-list)` can match zero characters, so in your UTF-8 string it can match “between” bytes. That means the replacement gets applied at each byte boundary, which is why the multibyte `ळ` gets split into invalid UTF-8.

Use `+(...)` if you want one or more matches, so it won’t match the zero-length gaps:

```bash
shopt -s extglob
printf '%s\n' "${str//+($'\x01')/ }"
```

Also, Bash pathname/glob operations are ultimately byte-oriented in many cases, because Unix pathnames are byte sequences, not guaranteed text. So this behavior isn’t unique to your pattern.

A `.so` file is a shared library, not a standalone program, so it’s usually not “executable” in the same sense as an app. It may have the executable bit set or contain loader-related sections, but that does not mean you run it directly like a normal binary.

Why it can *look* executable:
- Linux file permissions may mark it as executable so the dynamic loader can use it.
- Some `.so` files can also be built to be directly runnable for special purposes, but that’s uncommon.

In short: `.so` = shared library, `.a` = static library, and “executable” here mostly refers to file permissions or loadability, not that it’s meant to be run by itself.

`.so` files are usually shared libraries, and many are marked executable because:

- they contain machine code, so the OS loader may map them with execute permission
- the “x” bit on Unix means “may be executed/mapped”, not necessarily “is a standalone program”
- some `.so` files are directly loadable by the dynamic linker, and tools often set them executable for compatibility

So executable permission does not mean “run this as a program.” It just means the file can be executed or contain code that may be executed. Scripts and binaries both can have it, which is why `find -executable` catches them.

For a backup SSH account, don’t give broad file permissions or add it to sudo/admin expecting access to everything. Instead, use a dedicated key with a forced command.

`command="/usr/bin/sudo /usr/bin/rsync --server ...",no-pty,no-X11-forwarding,no-agent-forwarding,no-port-forwarding ssh-rsa AAAA...`

Better: allow only the exact backup command via `sudoers`:

`backups ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/rsync`

2. Add SSH public key:
`mkdir -p /home/backup/.ssh && chmod 700 /home/backup/.ssh`
`echo 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA...' > /home/backup/.ssh/authorized_keys`
`chmod 600 /home/backup/.ssh/authorized_keys`
`chown -R backup:backup /home/backup/.ssh`

3. Allow only specific command via sudoers:

4. If needed, force the command in `authorized_keys`:

This gives SSH access with very limited privileges.

The `root` user’s primary group usually has no special effect on privileges. UID 0 is what makes root all-powerful, not group membership.

Why it exists:
- Every user is expected to have a primary group.
- `root` group mainly provides a named group owner for files.
- On FreeBSD, `root` can have any primary GID, even one not listed in `/etc/group`, and still work normally.

So:
- `root` in `wheel` or `operator` doesn’t change what root can do.
- `wheel` matters for `su` restrictions on FreeBSD: only wheel members can `su` to root.

The “user group root” is just the root user’s primary group, usually with group ID 0. It does not automatically grant special extra rights by itself.

What matters is the user ID 0 account, root. Root has superuser privileges regardless of group membership. The owning group on a file mainly matters for traditional group permissions and ACLs, not for special system privileges.

So in practice:
- root user: special privileges
- root group: mostly a conventional/system group, not inherently privileged

If you meant a file’s owning group, it only affects access through permissions/ACLs, unless some specific configuration uses that group specially.

On Linux, `gid=0` only gives you membership in the root group, not root user privileges. So you generally **cannot** do tasks that require `uid=0` (effective root), such as:

- changing system files/ownership outside permitted access
- binding to privileged ports (<1024)
- mounting filesystems
- loading kernel modules
- changing network settings
- `kill`/signal processes you don’t own
- reading many root-only files

`gid=0` mainly affects **group-based permissions**. If a file or directory is group-owned by `root` and has group access, you may access it. But without `uid=0`, you don’t get superuser powers.

On Linux, if a process has GID 0 but not UID 0, it is **not root**. Group 0 alone gives very little extra power.

Tasks that generally **cannot** be done without UID 0 include:

- changing UID to another user (`setuid(0)`, `setuid(other)`)
- changing GID arbitrarily if not otherwise permitted
- mounting filesystems
- loading kernel modules
- changing system-wide network settings
- binding to privileged ports (<1024) unless capabilities are granted
- reading/writing arbitrary protected files
- changing most process ownership/priority settings

A process with GID 0 but non-root UID can only do things allowed by its UID, file permissions, and any capabilities it has. In practice, treat it as an ordinary user unless specific permissions/capabilities are granted.

On Linux, a process with uid != 0 but gid = 0 only has “group 0” privileges. It does not get full root powers.

Tasks/commands that will still fail include anything requiring:
- root uid specifically
- `CAP_*` capabilities only granted to uid 0/root
- changing file ownership (`chown`, `chgrp` to arbitrary groups)
- privileged mounts/device access
- binding to ports <1024
- modifying files where write permission is based on owner, not group

For your sshfs case, the mount is being shown as owned by `www-data`. Use id mapping so files appear under your uid:

`-o idmap=user,uid=<your_uid>`

The Linux kernel is a monolithic kernel, not a microkernel. That means most core services—process scheduling, memory management, filesystems, networking, and many drivers—run in kernel space. This usually gives Linux strong performance and simpler communication between components, but a larger kernel attack surface.

Microkernels keep only the most essential functions in kernel space, pushing drivers and services to user space. This can improve fault isolation and sometimes security, since a driver crash is less likely to bring down the whole system. The tradeoff is more overhead from message passing and more complex service interactions.

So, compared with microkernels, Linux generally favors performance and compatibility over the stronger isolation model microkernels aim for.

Inode-based file systems don’t avoid reboot because of the file system itself; they avoid needing a reboot after replacing library files because of how Unix opens files.

When a process loads a library, it gets a handle to the file’s inode (via the open file description). If you update the library by writing a new file or replacing it atomically, the old inode can still stay in use by running programs. New programs read the new inode; old programs keep using the old one until they exit.

So reboot is unnecessary because:
- the old library isn’t overwritten in place for active processes,
- running processes continue using the already-mapped old inode,
- new processes use the updated version.

A reboot is only needed if you want every process to pick up the new library immediately.

Inode-based filesystems don’t “replace” a file in place for running programs. They assign a file an inode, and processes use file descriptors/inodes, not the pathname.

So when you update a library:

- the old library file may be removed or replaced on disk,
- but any running process that already has it open keeps using the old inode/data,
- and any code already mapped into memory keeps running from RAM.

Newly started programs will see the new version, but existing ones continue with the old one until restarted. That’s why you usually don’t need a reboot for user-space library updates. Rebooting is mainly needed for kernel updates or when a service must be fully restarted.

2. Open `/proc/$pid/mem`
3. Use `lseek()` to the virtual address you want
4. `read()` the bytes
5. Detach

Example:
```c
int fd = open("/proc/<pid>/mem", O_RDONLY);
lseek(fd, (off_t)address, SEEK_SET);
read(fd, buf, len);
```

Direct access is often blocked by Yama/LSM settings and ptrace restrictions. If you just want memory inspection, tools like `gdb`, `pmap`, or `/proc/$pid/maps` plus `ptrace` are usually easier.

Today, there’s usually no real benefit or penalty to choosing primary vs logical partitions, as long as your OS and boot setup support them.

Historically, primary partitions mattered because:
- some older Windows versions had to be installed on a primary partition
- some systems required /boot to be primary

That’s generally not true anymore.

So if you’re using fewer than 4 partitions, either works. Many people simply:
- make the first partition primary
- put /boot there
- use logical partitions for the rest

That’s mostly a convention/personal preference now, not a technical requirement.

Primary partitions are chosen when you want a simpler, more direct partition layout, especially for booting operating systems.

Key reasons:
- Legacy BIOS/MBR systems can boot from primary partitions more easily.
- You can have up to 4 primary partitions total on an MBR disk.
- If you need more than 4 partitions, you usually use 3 primary + 1 extended, with logical partitions inside the extended partition.
- Some older tools or OS installers expect primary partitions for system/boot use.

In MBR:
- 1–4 = primary partitions (or one of these may be extended)
- 5+ = logical partitions inside the extended partition

So primary partitions are mainly for boot compatibility and simplicity; logical partitions are for exceeding the 4-partition limit.

`top` is showing what the scheduler reports, not “ideal” full saturation.

Common reasons you may see 97% instead of 100%:

- **Granularity/rounding**: CPU usage is sampled over time and rounded.
- **Kernel/system time**: some CPU time is reserved for OS work and may not show as your process usage.
- **Per-core vs total**: on a dual-core system, 100% in `top` may mean one core fully used, or sometimes normalized differently depending on settings.
- **Load balancing/scheduling**: your busy loop may not be continuously on the CPU due to context switches.

Also, your code has **undefined behavior** because `i` is uninitialized.  
`int` overflow itself does **not** affect memory; it only changes the variable’s value.

There’s no real contradiction: top is showing different kinds of memory.

- VIRT = total virtual address space a process can use/may have mapped. It can be large and doesn’t mean RAM is actually consumed.
- RES = resident set size, the part currently in physical RAM.
- SHR = portion of RES that is shared with other processes.

For actual memory pressure, look at RES, not VIRT.  
In your example, each php process has ~25–31 MB RES, so that’s the meaningful RAM usage. VIRT around 100 MB is normal and not directly comparable to RAM used.

Also, load average 250+ with 249 running means the system is heavily overloaded, even if RAM is still free.

- the filesystem uses a minimum block size (often 4 KB)
- a small directory still takes at least one block, so it shows 4 KB

Putting everything except `/home` on separate partitions is mainly about management and safety:

- Data separation: keeps user files, system files, logs, and temporary data isolated.
- Easier reinstall/upgrade: you can reinstall `/` without wiping `/home`.
- Space control: one area (like `/var` or `/tmp`) can fill up without taking down the whole system.
- Performance and quotas: different partitions can use different filesystems, mount options, or quotas.
- Security/reliability: writable areas can be separated from a read-only root, common on embedded devices.

Putting things like `Documents` or `Videos` on separate partitions is usually done for:

- **Easier reinstall/OS recovery**: you can wipe or replace `/` without touching data.
- **Data separation**: backups can target important data independently.
- **Space management**: large media files won’t fill the whole home filesystem.
- **Different filesystems/options**: e.g., encryption, quotas, performance tuning.

But there are downsides:

- **More complexity** with mounting and maintenance.
- **Nested mount points** must be mounted in order (`/home` before `/home/user/Documents`).
- If an upper mount fails, the lower ones won’t mount either.
- Files created in an unmounted mount point can “disappear” when it is later mounted.

For most users, a separate `/home` is enough; for subfolders, symlinks are often simpler.

Putting directories like /home, /var, /tmp, /opt, or /boot on separate partitions is usually for management and protection, not raw performance.

Common reasons:
- Limit damage from disk-full situations: if /var fills up, it won’t crash /home too.
- Easier reinstall/upgrade: keep /home and maybe /var while replacing the OS.
- Different backup/restore policies: user data in /home may need separate backups.
- Security/isolation: mount /tmp or /var with restrictive options like noexec, nodev, nosuid.
- Filesystem tuning: different usage patterns may benefit from different filesystems or sizes.
- Boot reliability: /boot may need a simple, early-boot-friendly filesystem.

It adds complexity, so many systems use only a few partitions unless there’s a clear need.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
shopt -s dotglob

for file in "$1"/*; do [[ -f "$file" ]] && d1+=( "$(md5sum < "$file")" ); done
for file in "$2"/*; do [[ -f "$file" ]] && d2+=( "$(md5sum < "$file")" ); done
```

- owner: `rw-` = `6`
- group: `r--` = `4`
- others: `r--` = `4`

The shell doesn’t “pipe” one redirect into the next. Each `>` simply reassigns the process’s STDOUT file descriptor.

So:

`cat test.txt > dummy.txt > dummy2.txt`

means:

1. run `cat test.txt`
2. connect its STDOUT to `dummy.txt`
3. then immediately re-connect the same STDOUT to `dummy2.txt`

The second redirection overwrites the first one, so only `dummy2.txt` gets the output. `dummy.txt` is just created/truncated, but nothing is written to it.

This is why redirection order matters, e.g.:

`find / 2>&1 >/dev/null`
vs
`find / >/dev/null 2>&1`

The first sends stderr to the original stdout, then discards stdout. The second sends both to `/dev/null`.

So the important part is not the spelling, but that `/etc/resolv.conf` contains DNS resolver settings. As in the related thread, tools like NetworkManager may rewrite it automatically.

“resolv” is short for “resolve,” not “resolved” or “resolver.” `/etc/resolv.conf` is the classic config file for DNS name resolution, so the spelling comes from that older Unix convention.

As for the thread context: a `domain` line is optional because `search` can already provide the lookup suffix list, and if `domain` is omitted, the resolver may derive a default from the hostname. In Linux, file permissions are shown like `drwxr-x---` or `-rw-r--r--`.

- First character: `d` = directory, `-` = regular file
- Next 3: owner permissions
- Next 3: group permissions
- Last 3: world/others permissions

Example: `-rwxr-x---`
- File
- User/owner: `rwx`
- Group: `r-x`
- World: `---`

`r` = read, `w` = write, `x` = execute/access

- first char: file type
  - - = regular file
  - d = directory
- next 3 chars: owner/user permissions
- next 3 chars: group permissions
- last 3 chars: world/others permissions

Example:
-rw-r--r--
= file
= user: read/write
= group: read
= world: read

drwxr-x---
= directory
= user: read/write/execute
= group: read/execute
= world: no access

Permission letters:
- r = read
- w = write
- x = execute (for directories: enter/traverse; for files: run)

So the “world, user, group” access is exactly the 3 permission blocks after the type character.

- `ip route` to see which interface has the default route
- whether both NICs are in the same subnet

```ksh
( your_command; print $? > /tmp/cmd.status ) | tee /tmp/cmd.log
status=$(cat /tmp/cmd.status)
rm /tmp/cmd.status
echo "exit status: $status"
```

If your ksh supports it, the usual idiom is:

```ksh

status=${pipestatus[0]}
```

But portability is better with the temp-file approach.

```sh
status=${pipestatus[0]}
```

If your ksh doesn’t have `pipestatus`, use a temp file:

But note: the `status` assignment happens in a subshell if you use a pipe directly, so it may not be visible outside.

```bash
status=${PIPESTATUS[0]}
```

`status` will contain the exit code of `cmd`, even though its output was piped onward.

Example:

```sh
try() {
  result=$(eval "$1" 2>&1)
  if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then

    echo "$result"

  fi

}

```

[`test` and `[` are usually the same shell builtin in POSIX shells; `[` is just the traditional command-name form used by `if` syntax. Example:

`if [ "$x" = y ]; then ...`

The builtin `[` requires a closing `]` as its last argument. That `]` is not an operator; it’s just syntax to make the command look like a bracketed test.

Differences:
- `[` is the test command name; it must end with `]`.
- `test` is the same functionality without the bracket syntax.
- Some shells also have external `/bin/test` and `/bin/[` versions, but builtin versions are faster and avoid subprocess overhead.

Also note: `[` is not a shell keyword; it’s a command.

When stdout is not connected to a terminal, many programs use block buffering, so `printf("foo\n")` may not appear immediately over SSH until the buffer flushes or the program exits.

Ways to fix it:

- In the program, flush after each print:
  `printf("foo\n"); fflush(stdout);`
- Disable buffering:
  `setvbuf(stdout, NULL, _IONBF, 0);`
- If you can’t change the program, use `stdbuf`:
  `ssh remotehost stdbuf -oL /path/to/test`
- For Python, Perl, etc., use their unbuffered modes.

SSH itself does not delay the output; the remote process does.

```sh
if [ -z "$first_byte" ]; then
```

Yes — the script can kill its own `grep`/`ps` pipeline or even itself if its name matches the search, which makes the script abort unpredictably.

Common fixes:
- Don’t parse `ps | grep`; use `pgrep`/`pkill` instead.
- Exclude the current PID with `$$`.
- If you must kill from inside the script, do it in a subshell and then exit.

Example:

```sh
for pid in $(pgrep -f script.sh); do
  [ "$pid" -ne "$$" ] && kill -9 "$pid"
done
```

Or:

```sh
( for pid in $pidsToKill; do kill -9 "$pid"; done ) &
exit
```

The key issue is self-matching/self-termination.

`kill` is getting the output of the pipeline as arguments incorrectly, so your script may be dying when `grep` finds its own process or when the command expands unexpectedly.

Use command substitution, and quote the pattern:

```sh
kill -9 $(ps | grep "server1" | grep -v grep | awk '{print $1}')
```

Or better, avoid `grep | grep -v grep` and use `pgrep` if available:

```sh
kill -9 $(pgrep -f server1)
```

If you want to prevent premature script aborts, also check that the PID list is non-empty before calling `kill`.

Your script is aborting because `kill` is seeing the `grep` process too, or because the pipeline is matching itself.

Don’t use `ps | grep | kill` directly. Filter out `grep`, extract PIDs, then pass them to `kill`:

```sh
ps -ef | grep "vmstat 1" | grep -v grep | awk '{print $2}' | xargs kill
```

If you want to be more careful, use `kill -TERM` or `kill -9` only if needed:

```sh
... | xargs kill -TERM
```

Also, if this is inside a script and `grep` can fail to match, make sure your script isn’t using `set -e`, which can stop execution on nonzero pipeline exit codes.

`root=/dev/ccl1` only works if the kernel knows that device name at boot. In your case it doesn’t, so it falls back to `00:00` and panics with “gave up waiting on root device”.

Best fixes:

1. Use the real kernel-recognized name, e.g. `root=/dev/hdc1` or `root=/dev/sdX1`.
2. If you want a custom name for scripts, create a symlink after boot:
   `ln -s /dev/hdc1 /dev/ccl1`
3. For modern kernels, use `root=UUID=...` or `root=LABEL=...` instead of a custom `/dev/...` name.

Also verify your custom 2.6.37 kernel includes the correct storage and filesystem drivers built-in, not just as modules, or it won’t find the root partition.

“Gave up waiting on root device” usually means the new kernel can’t mount your root filesystem because it lacks the right storage/filesystem drivers or has the wrong root= parameter.

Try this:

1. Rebuild the kernel config with:
   - `make oldconfig` before `make menuconfig`
2. Make sure these are built in or included in initramfs:
   - disk controller driver (SATA/SCSI/IDE, etc.)
   - root filesystem driver (ext4, ext3, xfs, etc.)
3. Verify grub uses the correct `root=` value and correct initrd.
4. Compare the new grub entry with the old working one.
5. Recreate initramfs after installing the kernel:
   - `sudo update-initramfs -c -k 2.6.37...`

If you still boot to the error, temporarily remove `quiet splash` to see which device it’s waiting for.

Your custom kernel is likely missing the partition-table support needed to parse `/dev/sda`, so it reports “unknown partition table” and never creates the disk partitions.

Check kernel config for:

- `CONFIG_PARTITION_ADVANCED=y`
- `CONFIG_MSDOS_PARTITION=y` for MBR disks
- `CONFIG_EFI_PARTITION=y` for GPT disks

If you need compatibility with other disk types, also consider `CONFIG_MAC_PARTITION`, `CONFIG_BSD_DISKLABEL`, etc.

These options are in `block/partitions/Kconfig`. If your root is on a normal PC disk, enabling MSDOS and/or EFI partition support usually fixes it.

This usually means the kernel can’t see the disk/controller for your root filesystem early in boot.

Check these first:

1. Make sure the needed storage driver is built into the kernel, not as a module. Common ones:
- SATA/AHCI: `CONFIG_SATA_AHCI`
- SCSI disk: `CONFIG_SCSI`, `CONFIG_BLK_DEV_SD`
- Your filesystem: ext4/ext3, etc.

2. Ensure initramfs is correct:
- After installing the kernel, run:
  `sudo update-initramfs -c -k 2.6.37`
  `sudo update-grub`

3. Confirm the root device name in GRUB matches reality:

4. If using a custom kernel, verify:

- `CONFIG_EXT4_FS` (or your FS)
- relevant SATA/RAID/AHCI drivers built-in

If you want, paste your `.config` root/storage settings and `lsblk`/GRUB entry.

- UUID: `/dev/disk/by-uuid/...`

Find them with:

If the kernel/initramfs is trying to mount `/dev/sda` and can’t find it, update your boot parameters or `/etc/fstab` to use UUID or label instead. That’s the standard fix.

It’s asking about CPU execution modes, not what a specific code snippet does.

Kernel mode:
- Full privileged access
- Can run any CPU instruction
- Can access any memory and hardware directly

User mode:
- Restricted access
- Must use OS APIs to interact with hardware
- Cannot directly access hardware

On most systems, this separation is enforced by the CPU itself (for example, x86 protection rings). It helps keep crashes in ordinary programs from bringing down the whole system.

`${3#?}` is Bash parameter expansion.

- `#` removes a matching prefix.
- `?` matches any single character.

So `${3#?}` returns the value of the 3rd argument with its first character removed.

Example:
- if `$3 = hello`
- `${3#?} = ello`

If `$3` is one character long, the result is empty.

- A missing dependency of one of the shared libraries.

In bash, `$?` only gives the exit status of the immediately previous command.

If you want the exit status of the command before that, you need to save it yourself before running the next command. For example:

```bash
prev_status=$?

echo "status before last command: $prev_status"
```

If you also need the previous command line, `fc` can show it:

```bash
last_command="$(fc -nl -1)"
```

- `-n` = no command numbers
- `-1` = the last command

If you want to save it to a file:

```bash
fc -ln -1 >> LOGBOOK
```

If you want a reusable helper:

```bash
getlast() {
  fc -ln "$1" "$1" | sed '1s/^[[:space:]]*//'
}
```

Then:

```bash
getlast >> LOGBOOK
```

This prints the command, but does not run it.

- **Supervisor** (`supervisord`) — runs as non-root, controls multiple processes, has CLI (`supervisorctl`), easy config.

Linux systems on multiple virtual machines can share the same swap partition only if they are not using it at the same time. A swap partition is just disk space, so multiple Linux installs can use it, but concurrent use can cause corruption or instability.

Important restrictions:
- The VMs must not run simultaneously if they share the same swap device.
- You cannot hibernate one VM and run another that uses the same swap space.

For virtual machines, the safer approach is to give each VM its own swap, or use a shared storage setup only if access is strictly exclusive.

You can’t fully “turn off swap” for just one process with cgroups. `memory.swappiness=0` only lowers the tendency to swap; it does not guarantee no swapping under memory pressure.

From the kernel docs:
- `memory.swappiness` affects a cgroup’s swap tendency.
- It cannot be changed for some cgroups (e.g. root or non-leaf groups).
- A value of 0 still allows swap in some cases.

If you need a process to never be swapped, use `mlock()`/`mlockall()` to pin its pages in RAM. For “less swap” on a specific group, place that process in a leaf cgroup and set a low `memory.swappiness` there.

If you want to fix only the swapping logic, use `awk` to swap every 1st and 4th pair in each block of 4:

```sh
... | awk -F, '{
  i=NR%4
  if (i==1 || i==0) print $2 "," $1
  else print $1 "," $2
}'
```

For your sample, that turns:

- `16,1` -> `1,16`
- `8,9` stays
- `15,2` stays
- `7,10` -> `10,7`
- `14,3` -> `3,14`
- `6,11` stays
- `13,4` stays
- `5,12` -> `12,5`

But the cleaner solution is to generate the imposition directly in bash, as in the accepted answer, instead of generating then swapping.

Bash does not expand `{1..$VAR}` the way zsh does. In bash, brace expansion happens before parameter expansion, so `$VAR` is treated literally inside `{...}`.

If you want the zsh-like behavior in bash, use something like:

```bash
eval "echo {1..$VAR}"
```

or more safely, avoid brace expansion and use a loop:

```bash
for i in $(seq 1 "$VAR"); do
  echo "$i"
done
```

So the short answer: none of the standard bash versions do this natively; zsh does.

`mv /tmp/folder/* /*` tried to move everything from `/tmp/folder` into the filesystem root `/`.

Because the shell expands `/*`, the destination is not a file but a list of paths in `/`, so `mv` may have:
- moved files into `/` using the same basenames,
- overwritten existing files if names matched,
- failed on directories/special files it couldn’t move,
- left open tmp files/sockets/pipes unchanged in running programs.

If anything in `/tmp/folder` had names like `bin`, `etc`, `usr`, `home`, etc., it could have scattered files into those locations and broken the system badly.

In zsh, brace expansion does not happen after variable expansion, so `{1..$VAR}` won’t work the way bash might.

Use a loop or `seq` instead, for example:

```bash
for i in $(seq 1 "$VAR"); do
  echo "$i"
done
```

If you want a zsh-native range with a variable, use arithmetic expansion:

```zsh
for i in {1..$((VAR))}; do
  echo $i
done
```

But note: plain `{1..$VAR}` is not reliably expanded in zsh.

In zsh, brace expansion happens before parameter expansion, so `{1..$VAR}` expands as text and then `$VAR` is substituted inside the range.

In bash, brace expansion is purely lexical and does not expand variables inside the braces, so `{1..$VAR}` will not work the same way.

There isn’t a bash option that makes `{1..$VAR}` behave like zsh. Use a loop or `seq` instead, e.g.:

```bash
for i in $(seq 1 "$VAR"); do
  echo "$i"
done
```

Or in bash arithmetic:

```bash
for ((i=1; i<=VAR; i++)); do
  echo "$i"
done
```

If you want zsh-style behavior, you need zsh.

`<<` is a shell “here-document” operator: it feeds a block of text to a command until a chosen delimiter is reached.

Example:
```sh
cat <<EOF
hello
world
EOF
```
This sends `hello` and `world` to `cat` as standard input.

`< <(command)` is different. It means:
- `<` = take input from a file/stream
- `<(command)` = process substitution: run `command` and treat its output like a file

So:
```sh
bash < <(curl ...)
```
means “run `curl ...`, and feed its output to `bash` as stdin.”

In short:
- `<<` = here-doc
- `< <(...)` = input redirection from process substitution

`<<<` isn’t a standard C/C++ operator. Its meaning depends on the context/language:

- In some shells (e.g. bash), `<<<` is a here-string: it feeds a string into a command’s standard input.
  - Example: `grep foo <<< "foo bar"`
- In some documentation or markdown, `<<<` can just be a literal text marker.
- In other languages/tools, it may mean something else entirely.

If you meant it in code, tell me the language or show the snippet and I can identify it precisely.

In UNIX/Linux shell syntax, `<<` is a here-document redirection.

It means: “take input from the lines that follow, until a line containing the delimiter appears.”

Example:

```sh
cat << EOF
hello
world
EOF
```

This sends `hello` and `world` to `cat` as standard input.

So:
- `<` = redirect input from a file
- `<<` = read input from the lines typed in the command itself, ending with the delimiter

`ps -f` is using the old UNIX-style option syntax, but on Linux `ps` accepts multiple option families for compatibility.

For `ps`, `-f` means “full format” in the classic UNIX sense. The reason Linux `ps` supports UNIX, BSD, and GNU options together is historical: Linux `ps` evolved from early implementations, and later gained compatibility with common BSD-style and GNU-style conventions.

So `ps -f` doesn’t mean “different representation of bash”; it just asks `ps` to display processes in full format. If you’re seeing `bash` listed differently, that’s the effect of the format selected, not a different process type.

In `ps` output, the number in brackets is usually the process’s **kernel thread ID / task number** or a **replacement name suffix** used by that `ps` implementation, not a shell argument.

For `init [2]`, it typically means `ps` is showing the process name plus an internal identifier to distinguish it from other tasks/threads, especially when the command name alone would be ambiguous or truncated.

So:

- `[...]` = “this is the process name, not argv arguments”
- the number inside = an internal task/thread identifier or disambiguator

Exact meaning can vary slightly by `procps` version and `ps` format, but it is not a bash option or command argument.

`ps -f` shows the command line as the shell started it, not the shell’s internal state.

So if you see `bash` with different arguments, that usually means one of these:

- Bash was started with options, e.g. `bash -l` or `bash --noprofile`
- The `ps` output is just showing the executable name plus its arguments
- You’re looking at a shell spawned by another program or script

If your goal is to change how a command behaves automatically, use an alias or function in your shell config, like the earlier example:

```bash
alias ls='ls -1'
```

For bash itself, you can’t “alias” its process representation in `ps`; that reflects how it was launched.

A shell can be:

- Interactive: it reads commands from you (a terminal). Typical use: working at a prompt. Files like `.zshrc` are usually for this.
- Login: it’s the first shell for a session, like after you log in via TTY, SSH, or a display manager. Typical use: set session-wide env vars; `.zprofile` / `.zlogin` in zsh.
- Non-login: any shell that is not a login shell. Typical use: subshells started from another shell. These often still can be interactive.

Important: interactive and login are independent. A shell can be both, one, or neither.

In zsh:
- `[[ -o interactive ]]`
- `[[ -o login ]]`

In bash:
- interactive: `case $- in *i*) ...`
- login: `case :$BASHOPTS: in (*:login_shell:*) ...`

- `who` or `w` — shows logged-in users and source host/IP

- `ps -ef | grep xrdp` / `ps -ef | grep sshd` — see remote access services
- For GUI remote access:
  - VNC: check the VNC server logs
  - X11 forwarding: check SSH logs and `echo $DISPLAY`

Quick definitions:

- Interactive shell: you type commands and get prompts. It reads user config like `~/.bashrc`.
- Login shell: the first shell after logging in. It reads login setup files like `/etc/profile`, `~/.profile`, `~/.bash_profile`.
- Non-login shell: any shell not started as the initial login shell. It usually doesn’t read login files.

Common cases:
- Interactive login shell: SSH login, console login, `su -`
- Interactive non-login shell: opening a new terminal window/tab, running `bash` inside an existing shell
- Non-interactive non-login shell: scripts, `ssh host command`

Use cases:
- Login shells set environment variables and session-wide settings.
- Interactive non-login shells are for day-to-day command use and aliases/functions.
- Non-interactive shells are for automation and scripts.

`scp -p` exists, but it only preserves times and modes; it does not reliably preserve all ownership/permission details like `cp -p` does locally. In practice, for copying between servers, `rsync` over SSH is usually the better choice:

`rsync -e ssh -aHS source target`

The `-a` flag preserves permissions, ownership, timestamps, symlinks, devices, etc. Note that preserving user/group ownership may require root privileges on the destination.

If you saw files being “modified” during `scp`/`cp`, that’s often because the copy operation updates timestamps or attributes as it writes the file.

Your file is being altered because you used `-t`, which allocates a pseudo-terminal on the remote side. PTYs do newline translation (`\n` becomes `\r\n`), which corrupts binary data and can also change file size.

Use SSH without `-t`:

`ssh me@server.com 'cat /path/to/foo.gz' > latest.gz`

If you need to identify the file first, do that in a separate command, then copy without a TTY. For binary-safe transfer, avoid anything that forces terminal processing (`-t`, `-tt`, `sed`, `echo`, etc.) and prefer `scp`, `sftp`, or `rsync` when possible.

If files are getting modified during `scp`/`cp`, the safer approach is to use `rsync`.

- To copy only newer files:
`rsync -au /local/directory/ host:/remote/directory/`

- To skip files that already exist in the destination:
`rsync -a --ignore-existing /local/directory/ host:/remote/directory/`

A few notes:
- The trailing `/` on the source matters. With it, contents are copied into the existing destination directory.
- `scp` and plain `cp` don’t have the same flexible “merge without overwrite” behavior as `rsync`.

If you want to replace a symlink with a real copy of its target, use:

`cp --remove-destination "$(readlink <symlink>)" <symlink>`

This works because:
- `readlink <symlink>` gets the target path
- `cp` copies that target onto the symlink path
- `--remove-destination` removes the symlink first, so the copy becomes a regular file

Then if you move the parent directory containing both the symlink and target together, the link still resolves correctly.

If you’re redirecting with `iptables -t nat -A OUTPUT ... -j REDIRECT --to-ports <localport>`, the packet’s destination becomes `127.0.0.1:<localport>`. So any filter rules allowing the original remote port won’t match anymore.

Allow traffic to the local redirect port instead, e.g.:

```sh
iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport <localport> -j ACCEPT
```

If `redsocks` connects out to the proxy, also allow that proxy IP/port on the normal interface, and make sure you bypass redirection for it to avoid loops:

```sh
iptables -t nat -A OUTPUT -d <proxy_ip> -p tcp --dport <proxy_port> -j RETURN
```

If you want, I can help write the full `iptables` + `redsocks` ruleset.

If you DNAT/redirect traffic to another host/port, that traffic is now considered “forwarded” from the firewall’s point of view, so it may be blocked by the FORWARD chain.

Allow it with a filter rule like:

iptables -A FORWARD -p tcp -d <redirected_host_ip> --dport <port> -j ACCEPT

If you only need local traffic to go to the new destination, the NAT rule is still:

iptables -t nat -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j DNAT --to-destination IP:80

Also make sure IP forwarding is enabled if the packet is leaving your machine:

sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

`chmod` uses octal mode bits. The leading digit controls special bits:

- `1` = sticky bit
- `2` = setgid
- `4` = setuid

So:

- `1777` = sticky bit + rwx for all
- `3777` = sticky bit + setgid + rwx for all

Both set the sticky bit because the `1` bit is present in the leading digit of each mode. `3777` just sets extra bits too.

On a directory, the sticky bit prevents users from deleting or renaming files they don’t own, even if the directory is writable.

The sticky bit won’t do what you want on a shared directory: it only prevents users from deleting files they don’t own, so owners can still delete their own files.

To allow some users to delete files while others cannot, use group permissions or ACLs instead:

- Put files/directories in a dedicated group, e.g. `smbdeleters`
- Add only the users who should be allowed to delete to that group
- Set directory permissions so that group members have write access and others do not

Example idea: set the shared directory to a mode like `575` for the intended access pattern, or use ACLs for finer control.

`EDAC MC0: UE page 0x0` usually points to a hardware memory error, not a driver bug.

- `EDAC` = Error Detection and Correction reporting from the memory controller
- `UE` = Uncorrected Error
- `page 0x0` often means the failing address decoded to page 0, which can happen with a bad DIMM, memory controller issue, or sometimes an address/reporting problem

It is generally **not** caused by a normal kernel module fault. A driver bug would more likely show up as a kernel oops/panic or module stack trace, not EDAC memory-controller errors.

Most likely suspects:
1. Bad RAM
2. Memory controller / motherboard issue
3. Less commonly, BIOS/firmware or platform reporting quirks

Check `dmesg`, ECC logs, and run a memory test.

`kernel: EDAC MC0: UE page 0x0` is usually a hardware memory error report, not a driver bug.

- `EDAC` = Error Detection and Correction framework
- `UE` = uncorrectable error
- `page 0x0` does not mean “address 0 is bad” by itself; it’s the page the kernel was able to map the error to, or sometimes a placeholder when details are limited

Most likely causes:
- failing RAM DIMM
- memory controller / CPU memory subsystem issue
- less commonly, motherboard or signal-integrity problem

It is usually not a normal software/driver problem. Check ECC logs / mcelog / rasdaemon, reseat or replace DIMMs, and watch whether errors repeat on the same slot/channel.

or replace `eth0` with your interface name. It can show link status, speed, duplex, and whether the adapter sees a cable.
